articles.title: After a decade of community pressure, LA bans oil drilling for good
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM For more than a decade, residents in some of Los Angeles’s most densely populated neighborhoods have lived alongside oil wells: down the street from active drilling operations, near idle wells leaking methane, in communities where benzene and hydrogen sulfide from nearby extraction have been connected to higher rates of […]
The post After a decade of community pressure, LA bans oil drilling for good first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

For more than a decade, residents in some of Los Angeles’s most densely populated neighborhoods have lived alongside oil wells: down the street from active drilling operations, near idle wells leaking methane, in communities where benzene and hydrogen sulfide from nearby extraction have been connected to higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function. On October 28, the LA City Council voted to end that. The ordinance bans new drilling immediately, prohibits the deepening or redrilling of existing wells, and requires all active operations within city limits to phase out over the next 20 years. Los Angeles is now the largest city in the United States to ban oil extraction, and the first to kick the industry out entirely.

A decade of community pressure

It took more than ten years to get here, and Wendy Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, has been campaigning with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood drilling, for most of that time. “Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade,” she said. For Miranda, the campaign was personal as much as political. She and her mother both have asthma, and many of the communities closest to the wells are working-class neighborhoods of color where residents have absorbed the health costs of extraction for generations. “Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health,” she said.

California’s oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world’s oil. Much of that production was in and around Los Angeles, and as the city grew outward, homes, schools, and businesses were built around the existing infrastructure rather than the other way around. Today, active wells sit near playgrounds, in residential neighborhoods, and along the coast. Idle wells, which under California law are those that haven’t produced oil for two years but can still return to production, dot the same areas. Residents near both report persistent odors, headaches, nausea, and breathing difficulties.

The legal setback that opened a new door

The City Council first passed an ordinance to phase out oil extraction in 2022, after sustained lobbying from residents including Miranda. Oil companies challenged it in court and won, successfully arguing that the city lacked the authority to impose a ban. California then passed legislation giving local governments broader power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations. The October 28 vote is what came out the other side.

Council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson was direct: “In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes. No one should have to live near an oil drilling site.”

The California Independent Petroleum Association has said it will challenge the new ordinance, calling it “an unlawful taking of private property” and arguing it will push residents toward greater dependence on foreign oil. The California Energy Commission has noted that the link between local production and pump prices involves crude costs, refining, transportation, and taxes, and that because oil is traded globally, domestic output doesn’t set what people pay at the pump. California’s production has been declining for decades in any case; output in the LA Basin is 43 percent lower than it was eight years ago.

Who pays for the cleanup?

The ban gets Los Angeles out of oil extraction, but what it doesn’t do is resolve what comes after. When wells stop producing, operators are legally required to remove equipment and plug them, but many haven’t. About 80 percent of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, roughly a third for over a century. CalGEM, the state agency overseeing oil and gas, collected just $1 million of the $36 million in fines it was owed in 2025. A Carbon Tracker report found that even if all future profits from California’s oil companies went toward decommissioning, the state would still face a $7 billion shortfall. That gap falls to taxpayers.

For Miranda and other advocates, the next phase is to compress the 20-year timeline and make the industry cover the cleanup costs rather than hand them off. She says she and her mother are both hopeful that future generations “can have better health and breathe cleaner air.” The council vote, in her words, “definitely represents hope.”

articles.title: ‘Make or bake time’: Guterres urges climate justice pact as leaders gather at COP31
articles.summary: UN chief António Guterres called for a new global climate justice agreement at COP31 on Wednesday, urging governments to tax fossil fuel companies to help countries bearing the brunt of a crisis they did little to cause. His appeal came as world leaders gathered in Antalya amid unresolved questions over climate finance and the future of fossil fuels.
articles.content:
Today at COP31

Leaders’ Summit: Guterres calls for climate justice and taxes on oil giants.

Guterres calls for climate justice and taxes on oil giants. Negotiations: Disagreements persist over adaptation finance.

Disagreements persist over adaptation finance. Zero Waste Day: Methane and innovative solutions headline the discussions.

Today saw packed corridors at the COP31 conference venue in Antalya as world leaders arrived for a two-day high-level Summit, bringing tighter security, road closures and an early start for delegates, some of whom reached the venue as early as 5 a.m.

Those who arrived before dawn were rewarded with a spectacular sunrise. Later, at the opening ceremony, traditional Turkish dancing, colourful performances, videos and even a COP31 theme song gave the opening ceremony an unusually festive air for a gathering confronting one of the world’s most pressing crises.

But the day’s most memorable message came from the Secretary-General, who accused polluters of delaying action, and once again warned that the climate crisis is advancing faster than global efforts to contain it.

“Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time,” he said, reminding world leaders that even if current national plans are fully implemented, the planet is heading towards more than 2.5°C of warming by century’s end.

But he insisted that breaching the 1.5°C threshold does not mean giving up. “Science is not telling us to surrender. It is telling us to fight harder” the UN chief said, stressing that every fraction of a degree of warming avoided matters.

Soundcloud

A new deal for climate justice

Against that backdrop, the Secretary-General proposed a ‘climate justice compact’ to help developing countries move away from fossil fuels while protecting those already suffering from climate change.

“We cannot demand that countries transform their economies while denying them the means to do so,” he said.

The proposed compact rests on four priorities:

Tweet URL

Accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels through national plans that protect workers and communities, while expanding renewable energy.

through national plans that protect workers and communities, while expanding renewable energy. Protect vulnerable populations with early-warning systems, stronger adaptation measures and faster support after climate disasters.

with early-warning systems, stronger adaptation measures and faster support after climate disasters. Deliver affordable climate finance , with wealthy countries fulfilling their commitments and more investment reaching developing nations.

, with wealthy countries fulfilling their commitments and more investment reaching developing nations. Strengthen international cooperation to overcome trade barriers, technological divides and geopolitical rivalries.

Polluters must pay

The UN chief took aim at fossil fuel interests, accusing them of distorting science and delaying climate action.

“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he declared. “The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do.”

He contrasted the $95 billion earned by the world’s nine largest oil companies in one quarter with the roughly $600 million received by the international fund helping vulnerable countries recover from climate-related loss and damage.

That was equivalent to just 14 hours of those companies’ profits, he said, urging governments to tax windfall profits.

“Polluters must pay”, a line that earned him an ovation in the plenary.

Leaders confront unfinished business

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, whose country is co-hosting COP31 in Antalya with Australia, acknowledged that three decades of climate negotiations had failed to deliver sufficient results.

“This success at the level of ideas has not produced the same results when it comes to implementation,” he said, calling for greater support for developing countries.

Brazilian President Lula da Silva, meanwhile, warned that climate change was losing ground on the international agenda as wars and trade disputes overshadowed the fight against global warming.

“We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival of future generations,” he said, defending international cooperation at a time when climate science and multilateralism are increasingly under attack.

Mr. Lula also announced that Brazil would develop national roadmaps to reduce its dependence on fossil fuels and end deforestation, building on the work of last year's COP30, which was held in the Amazon.

Feeding-the-biodigestor.jpg (19834)

Tackling methane: The ‘climate emergency brake’

An invisible gas that traps more than 80 times as much heat as carbon dioxide over 20 years featured prominently during Wednesday's “Zero Waste” thematic day.

Methane, released by fossil fuel operations, agriculture and rotting waste, is responsible for nearly a third of global warming to date. At a special event, Mr. Guterres called on the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) to develop a global standard for near-zero methane emissions from oil and gas.

UNEP is already tracking major leaks from space, using satellites and artificial intelligence to identify emissions and alert governments and companies.

Julia Ferini, who leads UNEP’s International Methane Emissions Observatory, told UN News that the system has helped reduce emissions in 45 cases across 13 countries.

She pointed to a recent case in Iraq, where a damaged gas pipeline had been leaking methane for two years, producing emissions equivalent to those of 350,000 cars. The leak was stopped by applying a coating to the corroded pipe.

“Methane is our climate emergency brake,” she said, explaining that cutting this short-lived gas could slow warming relatively quickly, buying time to reduce carbon dioxide emissions.

Yet despite more than 5,000 alerts issued since 2023, barely one in eight has received a response, the UN chief noted.

UNU-EHS/Austin Gonzales

Worms turning waste into something useful

And while negotiators in Antalya wrestle with how to accelerate climate action, young entrepreneurs are already putting some of them into practice.

In Botswana, Makwena Moesi is tackling food waste with an unusual workforce: more than half a million worms.

Her company, Viva Organica, collects organic waste from food retailers and turns it into fertilizer through a process known as vermicomposting, improving soil health while keeping waste out of landfills.

The business has already processed more than 1,000 tonnes of organic waste.

But Ms. Moesi, a biologist by training, says climate-friendly solutions must also make economic sense.

“A farmer does not wake up in the morning thinking about what am I gonna do to help sequester this amount of carbon dioxide from the air,” she told UN News.

Instead, she said, farmers want to know how much food they can grow, how to improve their harvests and whether they can afford the products that could help them.

articles.title: From Japan to Rwanda, early warnings are saving lives – but millions remain unprotected
articles.summary: Early warning systems are saving lives across the globe, but for millions of people the warning never arrives, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said on Wednesday, urging the world to protect every person on Earth by the end of 2027.
articles.content:
“No one should lose their life simply because a warning came too late – or never came at all,” he told a high-level event on the Early Warnings for All initiative at the COP31 climate conference, which runs until 20 November in Antalya, Türkiye.

His appeal came as a new report from the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) showed that 136 countries – 70 per cent of the total – now report having multi-hazard early warning systems, 17 more than in March 2025.

Tweet URL

Yet major gaps remain in the most vulnerable countries, as a powerful El Niño raises the stakes.

Warnings that worked

The report, Global Status of Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems 2026, finds that countries with substantial to comprehensive systems record disaster-related mortality 6.1 times lower than those with limited to moderate ones, and 3.2 times fewer people affected.

It also shows what that means on the ground. When a magnitude 8.8 earthquake struck off Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula in July 2025, the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center issued its first threat messages within 10 minutes.

Japan evacuated approximately 1.9 million people, while in Ecuador’s Galápagos islands, more than 2,300 people were moved out of high-risk areas hours before waves of about 1.3 metres reached the shore.

In Madagascar, an early action plan developed by the Malagasy Red Cross was partially activated before Tropical Cyclone Gezani made landfall in February, with some 600 door-to-door visits reaching 80,000 to 100,000 people with warnings and evacuation support.

And in Rwanda’s Karongi district, a tea farmer and her daughters were warned – through women’s cooperatives, SMS, local radio and loudspeakers – that heavy rain was expected within 48 hours, giving her time to reinforce her terraces, clear water channels and store her dried tea leaves before the downpour.

Gaps where risk is greatest

Around one in three countries still has no early warning system, Mr. Guterres said, with the widest gaps in least developed countries, small island developing States and countries affected by conflict.

“They did the least to cause the climate crisis, but are being hit first and hardest,” he said.

“Some European countries have more weather stations that meet global standards than the entire continent of Africa,” the Secretary-General added. “We cannot warn people about what we cannot see.”

WMO chief Celeste Saulo warned that the current El Niño “could be literally off our monitoring charts”.

“While we cannot stop El Niño, we can prevent many of its worst human consequences,” she said.

‘Build systems that last’

Urging countries to “accelerate and build systems that last”, Mr. Guterres set out three priorities:

making early warnings a permanent public service;

closing financing and capacity gaps; and

moving from fragmented projects to coordinated, long-term support for country-led plans.

Since 2022, some $2 billion has been mobilised and around 160 countries are receiving support, he noted. But finance must cover the entire warning chain, he said; “from weather forecasting to communication tools to volunteers knocking on doors”.

Warnings are also increasingly triggering action before disaster strikes: in 2025, 146 anticipatory action activations in 54 countries reached 9.6 million people, the report found.

“Countries have made significant progress in strengthening their early warning systems, but too many people remain unprotected,” said Kamal Kishore, head of UNDRR.

“The climate crisis is accelerating. Our protection of people must accelerate with it,” Mr. Guterres said. “Together, let us make sure that every warning arrives in time.”

articles.personality_title_fr: Les systèmes d’alerte précoce sauvent des vies dans le monde, mais des millions restent sans protection
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – De nombreux pays utilisent des systèmes d’alerte précoce pour prévenir les populations des catastrophes naturelles comme les tempêtes, les inondations ou les tremblements de terre. Ces alertes aident les gens à se préparer et à rester en sécurité. Pourtant, tout le monde ne reçoit pas ces avertissements, surtout dans les régions pauvres et vulnérables.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le Secrétaire général des Nations Unies, António Guterres, a souligné à la conférence climatique COP31 l’importance des systèmes d’alerte précoce. Un nouveau rapport montre que 136 pays possèdent désormais ces systèmes, soit 17 de plus qu’avant. Par exemple, le Japon a évacué 1,9 million de personnes avant un tsunami, et le Rwanda a averti des agriculteurs à temps pour protéger leurs récoltes.

**Impact** – Les pays avec des systèmes d’alerte solides enregistrent six fois moins de décès et moins de personnes touchées par les catastrophes que ceux avec des systèmes faibles. Cela montre clairement que ces systèmes sauvent des vies. Mais environ un tiers des pays, surtout les plus pauvres ou en conflit, n’en disposent toujours pas, exposant des millions de personnes au danger.

**Prochaine étape** – L’ONU souhaite que chaque pays ait un système d’alerte précoce permanent et bien financé d’ici 2027. Cela implique un meilleur suivi météo, une meilleure communication et un soutien aux communautés locales. Plus de financement et des plans à long terme sont nécessaires pour combler ces lacunes et protéger tout le monde.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Les systèmes d’alerte précoce sauvent des vies, et des efforts mondiaux urgents visent à étendre cette protection à chaque personne d’ici 2027.

articles.title: Can regenerative school gardens strengthen food security in Cameroon?
articles.summary: Students in Cameroon’s North West Region are managing school gardens and growing food using regenerative practices such as minimal tillage, composting, organic manure and fruit-tree grafting.
articles.content:
Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre in Ebang, Cameroon’s Centre Region, have recorded their first harvest of the 2026–2027 school year. Through the Climate Change and Innovation Club, an initiative introduced in 2024 by Support Humanity Cameroon (SUHUCAM) to connect environmental education with practical action, students planted huckleberry in their school garden at the start of the academic year in September. Like them, pupils in Cameroon’s North West Region are managing school gardens and growing food using regenerative practices such as minimal tillage, composting, organic manure and fruit-tree grafting.

Cameroon continues to face a decade-long humanitarian crisis, contributing to food insecurity in the Anglophone regions and Far North, while displacing thousands of families. Earlier this year, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies reported worsening hunger among nearly 6,000 Cameroonian households following an assessment. More than 3.3 million people were struggling to find enough food, while about 64 percent of households experienced severe food insecurity.

Children are among those affected. Nationwide, 29 percent of children under five experience chronic malnutrition. Beyond its nutritional consequences, food insecurity can also affect children’s ability to learn and participate in school activities.

According to the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), hunger can impair concentration and memory and affect classroom attendance. In February 2026, the organisation reported that only 2.8 percent of primary school pupils in Cameroon received a free hot meal at school, highlighting the limited reach of school lunch programmes.

Conflict, climate-related disasters, agricultural losses and rising staple food prices are among the main drivers of this crisis.

School gardens in action

To combat persistent food insecurity, educators and nonprofit organisations are partnering to teach children how to grow their own food.

In Bamenda, North West region of Cameroon, the Youth Association for Climate Action (YACA) runs the ADAPT Programme, which engages 70 pupils from two nursery and primary schools. Created after a survey revealed that few schools had gardens or provided environmental education, the ADAPT Club has established gardens with five sections: nurseries, vegetables, fruit trees, composting and tubers.

Muluh Kelly Vughose, Programme coordinator for ADAPT, says pupils are involved in more than just planting. “Our volunteers, together with the teachers and pupils, designed each garden. Children are also involved in learning basic agricultural skills like plantain propagation and grafting of fruit trees.” The club holds two sessions each week, lasting about two hours.

In the same region, in Nkambe and neighbouring villages, pupils from six primary and two secondary schools are learning agricultural skills through the Smart School Gardens Project, launched by Youth Development Organisation – Yodo Cameroon. Schools have received wheelbarrows, watering cans and compost manure to support the project.

“During the two years of implementation, I have watched these pupils and students care for plants from seed germination until harvest,” says Ekoaba Cevie, Yodo Cameroon’s Programme Coordinator. The gardens produce cabbage, huckleberry, carrots and Irish potatoes.

Meanwhile, SUHUCAM’s regenerative school garden programme in the Centre region combines fruit trees, including guava, soursop, orange and papaya, with plantains and produce such as huckleberry, cabbage and waterleaf. Through these activities, pupils are learning techniques such as composting, plant propagation and grafting.

Children are embracing the school gardens with enthusiasm, discovering the importance of food production and sustainability through practical experience. Queeninver Ngwangung, SUHUCAM’s Youth and Advocacy Lead, explains:

“Rather than simply teaching students about sustainable agriculture, food security or climate action, we give them opportunities to practice these concepts,” she said. “Through growing food, managing organic waste and caring for their gardens, we have observed that students have learnt that environmental solutions can begin with everyday actions within their own schools.”

For Amang Mael, a Form Three student, seeing vegetables grow on an abandoned plot behind his school has been particularly exciting. “Since we planted the vegetables, I have been so eager to harvest. We add organic manure to all our crops so they can be healthy.”

Another student, Kouba Princesse, believes the garden can contribute to the fight against hunger. “Now that I know how to grow my own vegetables, I will not have to depend on buying from the market all the time,” she says. Some kids have taken the practice home, where they maintain small gardens and use plastic bottles for drip irrigation during the dry season. Other students also say the experience has sparked an interest in pursuing careers in agriculture.

Supporting community nutrition

In 2025, the ADAPT Club produced approximately 45 kilogrammes of dry compost from biodegradable waste. At the end of each planting cycle, YACA organises a Mini School Garden Market Day, where parents and community members can buy the harvest. “Income gained is reinvested in the next planting cycle,” says Muluh Kelly.

At SUHUCAM, the harvests serve nutritional and educational purposes. Students eat fruits from the gardens, while vegetables are sold to purchase seeds and fund their continued management. Some students take extra produce home to establish household gardens.

After two years with two regenerative school garden cycles, SUHUCAM’s Climate Change and Innovation Club has benefitted thousands of households and planted over 400 trees.

In Nkambe, pupils involved in Yodo Cameroon’s project also sell their harvests to community members at affordable prices. The proceeds have helped schools purchase basic educational materials, including chalk and exercise books. Ekoaba Cevie, Yodo Cameroon’s project manager says:

The gardens have become practical outdoor classrooms. Not only are the children learning new agricultural skills, but they are also gaining an appreciation for nature, responsible environmental practices and sustainable resource management.

The nutritional potential of school-based production is also evident in other initiatives. In 2025, an integrated school production programme supported by FAO in Cameroon’s East and South regions established 18 school gardens. The programme produced 236,859 kilogrammes of vegetables, alongside eggs and fish, helping provide weekly healthy meals to 10,833 students. Children, teachers and community members also received training in sustainable agriculture, hygiene and nutrition.

Nkimih Clinton, a researcher at the Institute of Agricultural Research for Development (IRAD), says regenerative practices, such as those deployed in the community gardens, can improve soil health and support sustainable agriculture. Composting, mulching, crop rotation and organic manure, he explains, “can contribute to maintaining the health of pieces of land” for crop production. However, he cautions against expecting small-scale school gardens to eliminate hunger entirely.

Although they may not provide all the food pupils need, they can improve dietary quality by supplying vegetables, legumes and fruits rich in essential vitamins and minerals. “School gardens can be used as a source of production of micro-nutrients to complement basic staples (cassava, maize, rice) provided by parents,” Clinton says.

Challenges to overcome

Despite their benefits, maintaining school gardens remains difficult. Programme coordinators say unpredictable rainfall makes it harder to plan planting activities and sustain crop production. Changing weather conditions can also contribute to pest outbreaks and seed shortages.

Maintaining the gardens during school holidays is another challenge, as pupils are less available to care for the crops. These difficulties can interrupt children’s opportunities to follow the entire production cycle, from planting to harvesting. Expanding the initiatives will therefore require coordinated support from government officials, agricultural research institutions and development partners.

Schools need funding, reliable water supply, farming tools, quality seeds and technical assistance to maintain productive gardens throughout the year.

Government and policy support

Cameroon has previously taken steps to promote environmental education in schools. In 2018, the Ministry of Secondary Education and the Israeli Ambassador to Cameroon launched a Green School campaign that planted 300 trees in 30 schools.

In May 2023, the country launched the second phase of the Classes Vertes project, a three-year initiative developed by FAO in partnership with the Special Council Support Fund for Mutual Assistance (FEICOM) and several government ministries. Targeting 80 schools across the Far North, North, Adamawa, East and South regions, the programme sought to promote vegetable production, fish farming and poultry farming to improve children’s access to nutritious food. It also included tree planting and initiatives to build school canteens, water, sanitation, and hygiene facilities, with an allocated budget of approximately FCFA 722 million (USD 1.2 million).

The government’s commitment to improving children’s access to nutritious food is also reflected in its National School Feeding Strategy for 2025–2030, which aims to expand school meals and strengthen links between schools and local food producers.

Officials hope the program will reach one million learners by 2030. In July 2026, the government, through the Ministry of Basic Education, signed a EUR 3.6 million (USD 4 million) agreement with the World Food Programme (WFP) to expand home-grown school feeding in the Adamawa, East and Far North regions. The 2026–2029 programme is expected to provide nutritious meals to nearly 11,000 children in ten public primary schools while creating market opportunities for 600 smallholder farmers.

Meanwhile, experts believe school gardens can be replicated across Cameroon but stress that their implementation must reflect the country’s different agro-ecological zones. Rather than adopting a uniform approach, schools need solutions suited to their agro-ecological zones.

While school gardens may not independently resolve Cameroon’s food insecurity challenges, they offer opportunities to strengthen children’s nutritional knowledge, promote sustainable agriculture and encourage household food production. Their long-term impact, however, will depend on sustained investment, technical support and policies that enable more schools to establish and maintain these initiatives.

It highlights broad community impact, educational benefits, and government support, with detailed examples and measurable outcomes, making it a substantive and significant positive development in environmental education and food security.
articles.personality_title: School gardens in Cameroon teach kids to grow food and fight hunger
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Cameroon has been facing a long food crisis made worse by conflicts, climate problems, and high food prices. Many families struggle to find enough food, and nearly one-third of young children suffer from malnutrition. This also affects children’s ability to learn and go to school.

**What happened** – In several regions of Cameroon, students are now growing food in school gardens using methods that protect the soil and environment. Groups like Support Humanity Cameroon (SUHUCAM), Youth Association for Climate Action (YACA), and Youth Development Organisation (Yodo Cameroon) help schools plant vegetables, fruits, and trees. Kids learn skills like composting, grafting fruit trees, and using organic manure. They care for the gardens regularly and harvest crops like cabbage, huckleberry, carrots, and plantains.

**Impact** – These school gardens give students hands-on experience with growing food and show them how farming can be done in a way that helps the earth. The gardens provide fresh food for the students and their families, improve nutrition, and even generate small incomes when produce is sold. Children also develop a better understanding of nature and may be inspired to work in agriculture in the future. Community members benefit too, as schools sell vegetables at affordable prices and use money earned to keep the gardens going.

**What’s next step** – To keep and grow these programs, schools need more support like steady water, tools, seeds, and expert advice. The government is working on larger school feeding plans and partnerships with groups like the World Food Programme to provide meals and help local farmers. Experts say future gardens should fit the different farming conditions across Cameroon. With continued investment and careful planning, school gardens could reach more children and help improve food and nutrition in many areas.

**One-sentence takeaway** – School gardens in Cameroon are teaching children sustainable farming skills, improving nutrition, and supporting communities amid a food crisis, with growing government and local support.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des jardins scolaires au Cameroun enseignent aux enfants à cultiver leur nourriture et lutter contre la faim
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le Cameroun fait face à une longue crise alimentaire aggravée par des conflits, des problèmes climatiques et la hausse des prix des aliments. De nombreuses familles ont du mal à trouver assez de nourriture, et près d’un tiers des jeunes enfants souffrent de malnutrition. Cela affecte aussi leur capacité à apprendre et à aller à l’école.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Dans plusieurs régions du Cameroun, des élèves cultivent désormais des aliments dans des jardins scolaires en utilisant des méthodes qui protègent le sol et l’environnement. Des groupes comme Support Humanity Cameroon (SUHUCAM), Youth Association for Climate Action (YACA) et Youth Development Organisation (Yodo Cameroon) aident les écoles à planter légumes, fruits et arbres. Les enfants apprennent des compétences comme le compostage, l’implantation d’arbres fruitiers et l’utilisation de fumier organique. Ils s’occupent régulièrement des jardins et récoltent des produits comme chou, airelle, carottes et bananiers.

**Impact** – Ces jardins scolaires offrent aux élèves une expérience pratique de la culture alimentaire et leur montrent comment cultiver en protégeant la nature. Les jardins fournissent des aliments frais aux élèves et à leurs familles, améliorent la nutrition et génèrent même un petit revenu lorsque les récoltes sont vendues. Les enfants développent aussi une meilleure compréhension de la nature et peuvent être inspirés à travailler en agriculture. La communauté profite également, car les écoles vendent des légumes à des prix abordables et réinvestissent l’argent pour entretenir les jardins.

**Prochaine étape** – Pour maintenir et développer ces programmes, les écoles ont besoin de plus de soutien comme un approvisionnement régulier en eau, des outils, des semences et des conseils d’experts. Le gouvernement travaille sur des plans plus larges pour les repas scolaires et des partenariats avec des organisations comme le Programme alimentaire mondial pour fournir des repas et aider les agriculteurs locaux. Les experts recommandent que les futurs jardins s’adaptent aux différentes conditions agricoles du Cameroun. Avec un investissement continu et une bonne planification, les jardins scolaires pourraient toucher plus d’enfants et améliorer la nourriture et la nutrition dans plusieurs régions.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les jardins scolaires au Cameroun enseignent aux enfants des techniques agricoles durables, améliorent la nutrition et soutiennent les communautés face à la crise alimentaire, avec un soutien croissant des autorités et des acteurs locaux.
articles.personality_title_es: Jardines escolares en Camerún enseñan a los niños a cultivar alimentos y combatir el hambre
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Camerún enfrenta una larga crisis alimentaria agravada por conflictos, problemas climáticos y el aumento de los precios de los alimentos. Muchas familias tienen dificultades para conseguir suficiente comida, y casi un tercio de los niños pequeños sufren desnutrición. Esto también afecta su capacidad para aprender y asistir a la escuela.

**Qué pasó** – En varias regiones de Camerún, los estudiantes están cultivando alimentos en jardines escolares usando métodos que protegen el suelo y el medio ambiente. Grupos como Support Humanity Cameroon (SUHUCAM), Youth Association for Climate Action (YACA) y Youth Development Organisation (Yodo Cameroon) ayudan a las escuelas a plantar verduras, frutas y árboles. Los niños aprenden habilidades como compostaje, injerto de árboles frutales y uso de abono orgánico. Cuidan los jardines regularmente y cosechan productos como repollo, arándanos, zanahorias y plátanos.

**Impacto** – Estos jardines escolares dan a los estudiantes experiencia práctica en el cultivo de alimentos y les muestran cómo hacerlo de forma que ayude a la tierra. Los jardines proveen alimentos frescos para los estudiantes y sus familias, mejoran la nutrición e incluso generan pequeños ingresos cuando se venden los productos. Los niños también desarrollan un mejor entendimiento de la naturaleza y pueden interesarse en trabajar en agricultura. La comunidad se beneficia, ya que las escuelas venden verduras a precios accesibles y usan el dinero para mantener los jardines.

**Próximo paso** – Para mantener y expandir estos programas, las escuelas necesitan más apoyo como agua constante, herramientas, semillas y asesoría técnica. El gobierno está trabajando en planes más grandes de alimentación escolar y asociaciones con grupos como el Programa Mundial de Alimentos para proveer comidas y ayudar a agricultores locales. Los expertos dicen que los jardines futuros deben adaptarse a las diferentes condiciones agrícolas de Camerún. Con inversión continua y buena planificación, los jardines escolares podrían llegar a más niños y mejorar la alimentación y nutrición en muchas zonas.

**Frase clave** – Los jardines escolares en Camerún enseñan a los niños técnicas agrícolas sostenibles, mejoran la nutrición y apoyan a las comunidades en medio de una crisis alimentaria, con creciente apoyo gubernamental y local.
